Let’s dive into Chapter 8: Recognizing and Avoiding Accidental Diminishing.
You know, even the most well-meaning leaders can sometimes hold their team back—without even realizing it. These are what we call “Accidental Diminishers.” They honestly want to help, but sometimes their actions actually limit the growth and contribution of others.
There are a few classic patterns you might recognize.
For instance, there’s the Idea Guy—always tossing out new ideas, but unintentionally overwhelming everyone else, or making it tough for the team to think for themselves.
Then there’s the Rescuer, who steps in to help the moment there’s a struggle, but ends up taking away valuable learning opportunities.
Or maybe you’ve seen the Rapid Responder—quick to answer questions or solve problems, which can leave no room for others to figure things out on their own.
The Pacesetter sets such a relentless speed that others may feel they can’t keep up or that their contributions don’t really matter.
And finally, we have the Optimist, who’s always looking on the bright side. But by downplaying challenges, they can accidentally discourage people from voicing concerns or preparing for obstacles.
Here’s the thing: all these behaviors usually come from the right place—wanting to inspire, support, or protect the team. But the outcome? It’s just like more obvious diminishing. People disengage, their confidence drops, and they stop stretching themselves.
So, how can you steer clear of accidental diminishing?
First, try pausing before you jump in. Ask yourself—does the team really need your help right now, or would it be better to give them space to lead?
Next, focus on asking instead of telling. Use thoughtful questions to guide your team’s thinking, rather than always providing the answers.
Make it a habit to invite feedback. Check in with your team—ask how your actions are impacting their ability to contribute and grow.
And take a moment to reflect on your patterns. Notice when you tend to step in, and experiment with holding back just a little. It can make a world of difference.
For example, let’s say you’re a manager who always jumps in to solve problems. Next time, try waiting an extra moment before you respond. Give your team the chance to offer their own solutions. Over time, you’ll see them take more ownership and build real capability.
Recognizing accidental diminishing isn’t about beating yourself up. It’s really about building more self-awareness, and making small adjustments that can have a huge impact.
When you’re mindful of these patterns, your good intentions can truly multiply the intelligence and energy of everyone around you.
